title: Thailand’s semiconductor plan has a Washington problem
gist: Thailand's new 'Siam Silica' semiconductor strategy is well-designed on human-capital and capacity metrics but ignores US economic-security alignment (export-control enforcement), a gap the author says will cap its success since the US and allies represent over 90% of FDI into Southeast Asia's semiconductor supply chain (three-quarters for Thailand specifically) and China remains an insignificant investment partner.

themes.theme: Thailand's semiconductor competitive position and Siam Silica targets

insights.claim: Thailand is currently Southeast Asia's fifth-largest semiconductor exporter, exporting over US$10 billion of finished chips in 2024 — only 10% of Malaysia's and 6% of Singapore's exports — and has fallen behind second-tier exporters Vietnam and the Philippines, both of which exported less than Thailand as recently as 2016; by 2024 Philippine exports were more than double Thailand's.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Quantifies Thailand's declining relative competitiveness in Southeast Asia's semiconductor race — investors benchmarking regional semiconductor exposure should note Vietnam and the Philippines have overtaken Thailand.

insights.claim: Thailand's Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research, and Innovation launched the 'Siam Silica' semiconductor strategy in late July 2026, targeting one new fabrication facility, two additional advanced packaging facilities, eight integrated-circuit design companies, and training just under 3,000 new semiconductor specialists by 2030.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Concrete, trackable capacity-build targets (1 fab, 2 packaging facilities, 8 IC design firms, ~3,000 specialists by 2030) for monitoring Thailand's semiconductor sector progress.
insights.locator: paragraph on Siam Silica strategy details

insights.claim: New Lowy Institute research recommends prioritising regional cooperation and collaboration to drive stronger integration and avoid policy duplication as among the most effective interventions for Southeast Asian governments expanding semiconductor activities.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Endorses regional-integration strategy as the higher-value policy lever versus purely national semiconductor buildouts across ASEAN.

themes.theme: The US alignment gap as Thailand's binding constraint

insights.claim: Thailand's semiconductor strategy has one major barrier outside its scope: weak economic-security alignment with the US, since Washington's 'small yard, high fence' export-control policy sets red lines on Chinese access to US-IP-based semiconductors, and without a near-term shift in US priorities (which seems unlikely), Southeast Asian governments need to position themselves within the US economic-security umbrella.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: The core actionable thesis: Thailand's semiconductor ambitions are capped unless it tightens export-control alignment with Washington — a policy shift to watch for as a catalyst for accelerated FDI inflows.
insights.locator: paragraph on the major barrier to success

insights.claim: Southeast Asia, including Thailand, has been a consistent source of leakage for US export controls due to a lack of institutional capability to enforce sophisticated US-aligned controls, making the region a porous border enabling illegal smuggling of advanced semiconductors to China — a situation the author says is no longer sustainable.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Flags an enforcement gap that is likely to draw tightened US scrutiny or secondary sanctions risk on Thai/Southeast Asian entities involved in chip transshipment to China.
insights.quote: Southeast Asia, including Thailand, has been a consistent source of leakage for US export controls.

insights.claim: Malaysia has recognised the need for US alignment and made serious efforts to align with Washington's economic-security interests; Thailand has not, and the author argues Thailand needs to follow Malaysia's example to develop stronger semiconductor supply-chain capabilities.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Malaysia is presented as the regional benchmark for US-alignment strategy — a comparative case for assessing which Southeast Asian semiconductor hubs are better positioned to capture US-aligned FDI.

insights.claim: The US and its allies represent over 90% of total foreign direct investment into Southeast Asia's semiconductor supply chain since 2003; for Thailand specifically, that figure is more than three-quarters — meaning that despite declining regional trust in the US as a partner, it remains indispensable for semiconductors.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: A hard FDI-concentration statistic underscoring that US alignment is not optional for semiconductor investment capture in the region — critical context for assessing Thailand's investment-attraction strategy.
insights.quote: Collectively, the US and its allies represent over 90% of total foreign direct investment into Southeast Asia’s semiconductor supply chain since 2003. For Thailand, it is more than three-quarters.

insights.claim: China is transforming its indigenous semiconductor industry into an increasing source of competition for Southeast Asia even as ASEAN's semiconductor trade balance with China reverses and China remains an insignificant investment partner in the sector — leaving the region little choice but to align with the US and its allies on semiconductor supply chains specifically, even while resisting broader bloc alignment.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Distinguishes semiconductor supply-chain alignment (where US dominance is structural) from the broader US-China economic contest (where ASEAN stays non-aligned) — a useful nuance for sector-specific versus broad geopolitical positioning analysis.
insights.quote: While the region is resistant to choosing sides in the broader economic contest between China and the US, it has little choice when it comes to semiconductor supply chains.

insights.claim: The 2025 trade deals Southeast Asian governments signed with the Trump administration were the first explicit attempts to pull the region into Washington's economic-security orbit; while critical minerals were the initial focus, semiconductor supply chains represent the more substantial growth opportunity for Southeast Asia and a more economically consequential area for US partnership.
insights.speaker: Robert Walker
insights.so_what: Signals that 2025 US-Southeast Asia trade deals are a precursor to deeper semiconductor-specific alignment — worth watching for expanded chip-related provisions in follow-on agreements.
